title: Vibrato
concept:
Modulation does not have to go to the filter. You can route the LFO to any CV input — including the oscillator's frequency. When pitch wobbles up and down in a regular cycle, the result is vibrato: the same expressive technique used by violinists, vocalists, and guitarists.

A slow, subtle vibrato (rate around 5 Hz, low depth) adds warmth and life to a held note without sounding artificial. A fast, deep vibrato becomes more exaggerated — like a vintage electric piano or an old analog synth. At extreme settings it turns into a trill or a siren.

The key difference from filter modulation: here the LFO is affecting pitch, not tone colour. The note bends periodically above and below its target pitch. Combined with a slow attack on the envelope, the vibrato can be made to fade in gradually after the note starts — just like a real string player.

The LFO is running but not yet connected to the oscillator. Connect it to the Oscillator's Detune CV input — detune works in cents (hundredths of a semitone), so the vibrato depth stays proportional no matter which key you play.

task.instruction: Connect the LFO's output to the Oscillator's Detune CV input. Click the LFO's 'output' port (right side), then click the Oscillator's 'detune' input port (left side).
